title: A Review of the Research Literature on Evidence-Based Healthcare Design
review_question: To survey and evaluate the scientific research on evidence-based healthcare design and extract its implications for designing better and safer hospitals.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Rigorous empirical studies linking hospital physical environments with healthcare outcomes were included. The review built on a previous 2004 literature review, conducting a new and more exhaustive search, followed by a two-step screening process for relevance and quality of evidence.

evidence_base_summary.date_range: builds on a 2004 review, covering literature up to 2008

synthesis_conclusions: The state of knowledge of evidence-based healthcare design has grown rapidly in recent years.
Well-designed physical settings play an important role in making hospitals safer and more healing for patients, and better places for staff to work.

Improving outcomes for a range of design characteristics or interventions, including single-bed rooms, effective ventilation systems, a good acoustic environment, nature distractions and daylight, appropriate lighting, better ergonomic design, acuity-adaptable rooms, and improved floor layouts and work settings, is important.
The physical environment impacts nosocomial infection rates by affecting all three major transmission routes—air, contact, and water.
Infection rates are lower with very good air and water quality, and greater physical separation, isolation, or space per patient.
Providing accessible, alcohol-based hand-rub dispensers at the bedside can increase hand-washing compliance and reduce contamination spread by contact.
Medical errors are caused by a combination of people and the environment, and environmental approaches can play an important role in reducing errors.
Environmental factors like noise, light, and acuity-adaptable single-patient rooms are related to medical errors.
Exposing patients to nature can produce substantial and clinically important alleviation of pain.
Patients experience less pain when exposed to higher levels of daylight.
Sleep disruption and deprivation are very common problems in healthcare settings, especially for high-acuity patients.
Environmental factors such as noise and light may result in electroencephalographic arousals and awakenings, fragmenting sleep.
Stress experienced by patients is an important negative outcome, directly and adversely affecting many other healthcare outcomes.
Real or simulated views of nature can produce substantial restoration from psychological and physiological stress within a few minutes.
Gardens in hospitals can reduce stress among patients and families by providing nature distraction and fostering social support.
Noise is a pervasive stressor that elevates psychological and physiological stress in patients.
The great majority of patients prefer and respond positively to representational nature art, but abstract or ambiguous art can elicit stressful reactions.
Exposure to bright artificial light and daylight is effective in reducing depression and improving mood.
Patients with depression can have more favorable recovery outcomes, including shorter stays, if assigned to sunnier rooms.
There is limited literature directly linking physical environments to length of stay, but light and nature views have consistently shown a positive impact.
Wayfinding problems in hospitals are costly and stressful, particularly for outpatients and visitors.
An integrated wayfinding system, including coordinated elements like signs, verbal directions, and physical setting, is crucial.
Inadequate privacy may lower patient satisfaction and worsen healthcare outcomes.
Single-bed rooms provide better protection for patient speech privacy compared to multibed rooms.
Communication among patients, family, and staff is important for social support, family involvement in care, and patient satisfaction.
Single-patient rooms and private discussion areas can facilitate communication.
Social support reduces families' stress, anxiety, and depression, and increases their satisfaction with the hospital stay.
Environmental satisfaction is a significant predictor of overall satisfaction in healthcare settings.
Hospital workers experience a high rate of occupational injury, especially musculoskeletal injuries.
Ceiling lifts consistently reduce the incidence and cost of staff injuries.
High workplace stress contributes to employee burnout and intention to leave the job for healthcare providers, especially nurses.
Environmental factors associated with staff stress include noise, light, and single- versus multibed patient rooms.
Improved hospital design can make the jobs of staff easier, affecting unit configuration, noise, and other distractions.
evidence_gaps: Precise specification of minimum ventilation and filtration requirements for certain patient groups and treatment spaces, or maximum tolerable level of spores per cubic meter for airborne transmission.
Cost-benefit research for laminar airflow (LAF) effectiveness in patient-care areas near construction/renovation sites.
Studies systematically varying the number and location of alcohol hand-rub dispensers to isolate their independent effect on hand-washing compliance and infection rates.
Studies defining accessible locations for hand-washing facilities based on empirical analysis of staff movement paths, visual fields, patient/family interactions, and work processes.
Clear-cut and fully resolved understanding of advantages/disadvantages of carpeting versus other floor coverings for infection control.
Empirical evidence linking point-of-use water fixtures to nosocomial infections, and consensus on disinfection/removal for general use.
Empirical documentation linking properly maintained decorative fountains to hospital-acquired infections.
Further confirmation of findings on environmental factors reducing medical errors, and identification of ways to design better working environments to prevent errors.
Testing the impact of different auditory factors on medical errors under real-life conditions.
More complete understanding of the effectiveness of decentralized nurse stations and single-bed rooms in reducing patient falls and their implications for designing safe patient-care units.
Better understanding of how both daytime and nighttime light environments can be optimized to improve sleep.

Future research on sleep should control for variables like acuity of illness, sedation level, pain, and disruptive patient-care procedures, using longitudinal designs with larger patient numbers and 24-hour sleep measures.
More research in diverse settings with various patient populations to examine the contribution of nature views to overall healing process and length of stay.
Research directly assessing the comparative performance of different wayfinding systems or their impact on other healthcare outcomes.
Ascertaining the magnitude of stress created by wayfinding problems for outpatients and family members.
Future studies on speech privacy using more sensitive and advanced acoustic measures, such as the privacy index (PI).
Further exploration of environment-communication relationships in more diverse healthcare settings and how design measures can enhance communication.
More evidence linking design features to the level or quality of social support.
More research to understand whether ceiling lifts can reduce staff injuries from repositioning patients.
More research to understand the impact of natural light on staff stress.
More studies examining the effects of environmental factors on job satisfaction.
heterogeneity_sources: Most changes of the physical environment in healthcare settings alter several environmental factors simultaneously, creating confounding variables.
Many studies are not well controlled (e.g., observational studies without control groups).
Different measures used across sleep studies make findings difficult to compare.
Multifaceted interventions make it difficult to attribute effectiveness to a single design factor (e.g., hand-washing, patient handling programs).
Conflicting findings on certain environmental factors (e.g., carpeting, noise levels in ORs).

moderators.effect: Nurses from ICUs, EDs, or ORs were mostly exposed to daylight for less than 3 hours, while nurses from inpatient units mostly had an exposure of more than 3 hours, complicating findings on daylight exposure and staff stress/satisfaction.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Different daylight exposure durations for different nursing roles.

limitations: Relatively few randomized controlled trials linking specific design features or interventions directly to healthcare outcomes.
Most changes in the physical environment alter several environmental factors simultaneously, making it difficult to disentangle independent effects.
The largest category of studies consisted of observational studies with or without control groups.
Many studies are not well controlled.
Lack of precise specification for some environmental parameters (e.g., ventilation requirements, spore levels).
Difficulty in isolating the independent role of single design factors due to multifaceted interventions.
Limited cost-benefit research for certain interventions.
Conflicting research findings on some environmental surface materials.
Limited empirical evidence for some proposed links (e.g., water fountains to infection).
Generalizability of some experimental findings (e.g., noise impact on surgeons).
The review itself is a narrative review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis, which inherently has limitations in quantitative synthesis and bias assessment.
